questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Define what an allele is
questions.stem: A design brief for a seed-breeding line asks the team to define what an allele is before choosing parental plants.

options.text: An allele is one of the alternative versions of a gene that occupy the same locus on a chromosome.
An allele is a physical copy of a gene that can leave the nucleus and travel into the cytoplasm.
options.misconception: confuses a gene copy with an organelle

options.text: An allele is the observable trait an organism displays when it is grown under one particular environment.
options.misconception: mistakes a phenotype for a genetic variant

options.text: An allele is the pairing of one maternal and one paternal gene that sits together inside one cell.
options.misconception: thinks homologous chromosomes form a single allele pair

questions.explanation: An allele is a version of a gene, not a location or a trait. Genes stay in the nucleus in eukaryotes, and a phenotype reflects environment as well as genotype.
questions.hint: Think of alleles as alternative versions of one gene.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish genotype from phenotype
questions.stem: Brief reviewers insist the design review board distinguish a plant's genotype from its phenotype.

options.text: The genotype is what the plant looks like, and the phenotype is the gene pair it inherited from its parents.
options.misconception: reverses genotype and phenotype when naming them

options.text: The genotype is the allele combination the plant carries, while the phenotype is how it appears.
The genotype is fixed by the environment, and the phenotype changes whenever the plant is moved outdoors.
options.misconception: believes the environment sets the allele combination

options.text: The genotype and the phenotype are two names for the same inherited information, used in different documents.
options.misconception: treats genotype and phenotype as identical labels

questions.explanation: Genotype is the allele combination carried; phenotype is the trait that combination produces. Environment can shift how a genotype is expressed, so related but never identical.
questions.hint: Ask which one names the genes rather than the traits.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Apply segregation to explain a gamete split
questions.stem: A validation brief reports that a tall pea plant crossed with a short one produced 62 tall and 58 short offspring, and asks what separates.

options.text: Each offspring receives one tall allele and one short allele, so all should look the same height.
options.misconception: believes every gamete carries both alleles at once

options.text: The tall parent must be homozygous, because a heterozygous plant could never give an identical offspring.
options.misconception: assumes a heterozygous parent cannot make identical gametes

options.text: The two alleles separate during fertilization only, so gametes from each parent stay genetically identical.
options.misconception: puts allele separation only at fertilization time

options.text: The two alleles of the gene separate when gametes form, so each gamete carries just one of them.

questions.explanation: Segregation means the two alleles of a gene separate when gametes form, so each gamete receives one allele. The 62:58 near 1:1 split matches a heterozygous tall parent with a homozygous short one.
questions.hint: Ask which stage of cell division the split occurs in.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what dominance does and does not mean
questions.stem: A lab brief is rejected because a draft claims a dominant allele always produces a stronger trait than a recessive one.

options.text: The draft is right, because dominance guarantees the dominant phenotype is more extreme in every environment.
options.misconception: believes dominance guarantees a stronger physical effect

options.text: The draft should say dominance means the recessive allele is absent from every gamete the organism makes.
options.misconception: thinks the recessive allele is never passed on

options.text: The draft confuses dominance with intensity; dominance only says one allele masks the other's expression.
The draft should say both alleles are always expressed together in a heterozygote, making them equivalent.
options.misconception: claims heterozygotes express both alleles equally

questions.explanation: Dominance describes which allele shows in a heterozygote, not how strong the trait is. A dominant trait can be milder than a recessive one, and both alleles are still inherited.
questions.hint: Separate which allele shows from how strong it is.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a recessive fraction for a monohybrid cross
questions.stem: One requirement in the brief asks for the fraction of F2 offspring showing the recessive phenotype from a monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes.
questions.explanation: In an Aa by Aa cross the genotypic ratio is 1:2:1, so a quarter of offspring are homozygous recessive and show the recessive trait. The recessive allele passes with probability 0.5 times 0.5, which is 0.25.
questions.hint: Use the product rule on the two gametes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a two-trait probability for a dihybrid cross
questions.stem: Another requirement in a design brief asks for the probability that a seed shows both dominant traits in a dihybrid cross.
questions.explanation: Each trait shows with probability three quarters in a double heterozygous cross, and the two genes assort independently. Multiplying 0.75 by 0.75 gives 0.5625 for offspring showing both dominant traits.
questions.hint: Multiply the two single-trait probabilities together.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a testcross reveals an unknown genotype
questions.stem: The writing team must explain in writing how a testcross reveals the genotype of an unknown plant.

answer.exemplar: A testcross mates the unknown plant with a homozygous recessive individual. If the unknown plant is homozygous dominant, every offspring shows the dominant trait; if it is heterozygous, the offspring split about 1:1 between dominant and recessive phenotypes.

questions.explanation: The tester supplies only recessive alleles, so dominant offspring must take a dominant allele from the unknown parent. All dominant offspring implies homozygous dominant; a 1:1 split implies heterozygous.
questions.hint: Name the phenotype the tester parent always shows.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a 3:1 ratio is an expectation
questions.stem: A design brief asks why the classic 3:1 phenotype ratio does not appear in every F2 generation.

options.text: Because a 3:1 split assumes equal survival of all four phenotypes, which most experiments cannot guarantee.
options.misconception: blames unequal survival rather than expected probabilities

options.text: Because the ratio applies only to genotypes, and phenotype counts depend on how the plants are labelled.
options.misconception: claims the ratio describes genotypes and not phenotypes

options.text: Because a 3:1 ratio is an expected statistical outcome from random gamete pairing, not a guarantee.
Because dominant traits mask recessive ones only in a full dihybrid cross, not in a single-gene cross.
options.misconception: restricts dominance effects to dihybrid crosses only

questions.explanation: The 3:1 ratio is the expected outcome of a monohybrid cross with many offspring, based on random gamete combinations. Small broods vary around that expectation, and non-Mendelian genes would change it.
questions.hint: Think about sampling size and random pairing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Relate genotypic and phenotypic ratios
questions.stem: Brief writers must explain to reviewers why the genotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross differs from the phenotypic one.

options.text: Genotypic and phenotypic ratios always match exactly whenever only one gene is involved in a cross.
options.misconception: believes both ratios must coincide in every monohybrid cross

options.text: The genotypic ratio 1:2:1 splits into dominant and recessive phenotypes in the proportion 3:1.
The genotypic ratio is fixed at one half while the phenotypic ratio varies with the environment each plant meets.
options.misconception: claims the genotypic ratio shifts with the environment

options.text: The genotypic ratio depends on the colour of the seed coats, so it can never be written as a simple ratio.
options.misconception: ties the genotypic ratio to visible seed coat colour

questions.explanation: The 1:2:1 genotypic ratio has three categories, while the 3:1 phenotypic ratio merges the two genotypes sharing the dominant phenotype. One quarter plus one half makes the dominant class.
questions.hint: Merge the two genotypes that look alike.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Test a dihybrid harvest against the expected ratio
questions.stem: A brief reports 480 maize ears from a dihybrid cross, of which 270 showed both dominant traits, 120 only the first, 72 only the second and 18 neither.

options.text: The observed fractions match the expected 9:3:3:1 ratio for a dihybrid cross between two double heterozygotes.
The counts show a 3:1 ratio, so the brief should state that only one gene is segregating in this cross.
options.misconception: reads a three to one split into a dihybrid harvest

options.text: The counts match the expected 1:2:1 ratio, so the brief should report the result as a single-gene cross.
options.misconception: applies a single-gene genotypic ratio to two traits

options.text: The counts fit no standard ratio, so the brief should claim that the two genes are linked and always inherited together.
options.misconception: assumes any deviation proves the genes are fully linked

questions.explanation: Twice the 9:3:3:1 ratio predicts 288:96:96:32 among 480 offspring, close to the observed counts. The genes assort independently, and the product rule gives nine sixteenths double dominant.
questions.hint: Scale the nine to three to three to one ratio.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct an error about gene copies in somatic cells
questions.stem: One paragraph in the brief is sent back for rewrite because it describes the two copies of a gene in a somatic cell as identical always.

options.text: The brief is correct, because a somatic cell always holds two identical copies of every gene it carries.
options.misconception: assumes every gene copy in a somatic cell must be identical

options.text: The brief should say that somatic cells carry only one copy of each gene to save space and speed repair.
options.misconception: believes somatic cells halve their gene copy number

options.text: The brief should say identical copies are the norm and different alleles occur only in gametes.
options.misconception: restricts allelic variation to gametes alone

options.text: The brief is wrong, because the two copies of a gene in a diploid cell can carry different alleles.

questions.explanation: A diploid somatic cell holds two copies of each gene, one from each parent, and they may carry different alleles. Identical copies occur only in homozygotes, so the brief misstates genotype.
questions.hint: Recall which genotypes give two identical copies.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the homozygous dominant probability
questions.stem: The design brief asks the team to calculate the probability that an F2 offspring is homozygous dominant for the trait of interest.
questions.explanation: Two heterozygotes produce a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio in which the homozygous dominant class is one part in four. Each gamete carries the dominant allele with probability 0.5, and 0.5 times 0.5 gives 0.25.
questions.hint: Apply the product rule to both gametes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count expected recessive offspring from a cross
questions.stem: A brief asks how many offspring of 200 are expected to show the recessive trait in a cross of two heterozygotes.
questions.explanation: A cross of two heterozygotes gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio, so one quarter of the 200 offspring should show the recessive trait. Multiplying 200 by 0.25 gives an expected 50 recessive individuals.
questions.hint: Take one quarter of the total offspring count.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe the definition and limits of dominance
questions.stem: For a section on dominance the brief asks the team to describe in writing what dominance is and what it does not determine.

answer.exemplar: Dominance means that in a heterozygote the phenotype shows the effect of one allele, the dominant one, while the recessive allele is masked. It says nothing about how strong or weak the trait is, and it does not make the recessive allele disappear from the genotype or from the gametes the organism passes on.

questions.explanation: Dominance is the relationship between two alleles of one gene in a heterozygote. It fixes which phenotype appears, not how strong the trait is, and it never removes the recessive allele.
questions.hint: Think about what a heterozygote actually shows.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Define a monohybrid cross
questions.stem: A design brief asks the team to describe what a monohybrid cross is before the pilot planting begins.

options.text: A cross that follows the inheritance of a single gene with two contrasting alleles.
A cross in which two pairs of genes are studied together, so offspring show a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
options.misconception: describes a dihybrid cross with two gene pairs

options.text: A cross between two individuals that differ in only one observable trait and one invisible trait.
options.misconception: believes the number of traits must be even

options.text: A cross in which one parent is used repeatedly to generate identical offspring for a control plot.
options.misconception: describes repeated backcrossing rather than a monohybrid

questions.explanation: A monohybrid cross follows one gene with two alleles, giving the 1:2:1 genotypic and 3:1 phenotypic ratios. The name counts gene pairs, not visible traits, and offspring number is unlimited.
questions.hint: Count the gene pairs being followed, not the traits.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why four phenotypes arise in a dihybrid cross
questions.stem: Brief reviewers want to know why a dihybrid cross of two double heterozygotes produces four phenotypes.

options.text: Four phenotypes appear because each trait is controlled by two genes rather than one gene in every case.
options.misconception: claims each trait is controlled by two separate genes

options.text: Four phenotypes appear because two independently assorting genes each split into dominant and recessive classes.
Four phenotypes appear because the brief orders the four alleles instead of arranging them in pairs.
options.misconception: confuses allele pairs with a simple list of alleles

options.text: Four phenotypes appear because incomplete dominance always splits each dominant trait into two halves.
options.misconception: assumes incomplete dominance is the normal case

questions.explanation: Each of the two genes contributes a dominant or recessive class, and independent assortment lets both combine freely, giving two times two, or four phenotype classes, with expected proportions 9:3:3:1.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of classes for each gene.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Infer genotype from testcross offspring counts
questions.stem: A brief tabulates a testcross of an unknown purple plant with a white tester and records 44 purple and 46 white offspring.

options.text: The unknown plant must be homozygous dominant, because every tester allele is masked in the offspring.
options.misconception: confuses masked tester alleles with a homozygous unknown

options.text: The unknown plant must be homozygous recessive, because a purple parent cannot make white offspring.
options.misconception: thinks a dominant parent cannot produce recessive offspring

options.text: The unknown plant produced two different gamete types because the white tester also carried a dominant allele.
options.misconception: invents a dominant allele in the homozygous tester

options.text: The unknown plant is heterozygous, because offspring show both the dominant and recessive phenotypes.

questions.explanation: In a testcross the recessive tester contributes only recessive alleles, so a 44:46 near 1:1 split means the unknown parent made equal numbers of dominant and recessive gametes. Only a heterozygous unknown can do that.
questions.hint: Count the two phenotype classes in the testcross.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Reject the claim that ratios are exact counts
questions.stem: A brief is challenged because it claims a 3:1 phenotypic ratio must appear exactly in every small brood.

options.text: The brief is right, because Mendelian ratios are fixed counts that never shift between broods.
options.misconception: treats an expected ratio as an exact count every time

options.text: The brief should say that small broods always show exactly one quarter recessive and never fewer.
options.misconception: claims the recessive class never falls below one quarter

options.text: The brief is wrong, because 3:1 is an expected ratio for large numbers and small broods vary around it.
The brief should say that only broods larger than a thousand seedlings can show a Mendelian ratio.
options.misconception: insists on a fixed minimum brood size for ratios

questions.explanation: Ratios describe expected proportions, so a small brood of ten seedlings can easily show 7:3 or even 10:0 by chance. Only with large numbers does the observed proportion settle close to the expected 3 to 1.
questions.hint: Remember what ratios predict versus guarantee.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count homozygous dominant seedlings from a ratio
questions.stem: A brief asks the team to calculate how many of 240 seedlings would be homozygous dominant in a cross of two heterozygotes.
questions.explanation: The genotypic ratio from two heterozygotes is 1:2:1, so one quarter of the seedlings are homozygous dominant. One quarter of 240 is 60, so the brief should forecast 60 homozygous dominant seedlings.
questions.hint: One quarter of the total is homozygous dominant.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a dominant phenotype probability
questions.stem: A brief asks for the probability that an offspring shows the dominant trait when two heterozygotes are crossed.
questions.explanation: Multiplying the two gamete probabilities gives 0.5 times 0.5, or 0.25, for the recessive phenotype. The dominant phenotype therefore occurs with probability 1 minus 0.25, which is 0.75.
questions.hint: Multiply for the recessive case, then subtract.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how alleles relate to a gene in a diploid cell
questions.stem: A written section in the brief asks the team to explain how alleles relate to one gene in a diploid cell.

answer.exemplar: A gene is a stretch of DNA at a fixed locus, and an allele is one of the versions of that gene found in the population. A diploid cell holds two of these versions, one inherited from each parent, and they may be the same allele in a homozygote or different alleles in a heterozygote.

questions.explanation: Alleles are alternative versions of a single gene at one locus, and a diploid cell carries two of them, one per parental chromosome set. Those two may match, giving a homozygote, or differ, giving a heterozygote.
questions.hint: Define the gene first, then the versions of it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State the difference between genotype and phenotype
questions.stem: The requirements section asks the team to distinguish genotype from phenotype in the build specification.

options.text: Genotype is the allele pair an organism carries, while phenotype is the trait that pair produces.
Genotype is the appearance of the organism, while phenotype is the allele pair inherited from its parents.
options.misconception: reverses genotype and phenotype when naming them

options.text: Genotype and phenotype are separate names for the same inherited information.
options.misconception: treats genotype and phenotype as identical labels

options.text: Genotype is fixed by the environment, while phenotype stays constant across all conditions.
options.misconception: believes the environment sets the allele combination

questions.explanation: Genotype names the alleles carried, phenotype names the resulting trait, and the environment can alter how a genotype is expressed. The two are related but never interchangeable.
questions.hint: Ask which term refers to the inherited allele pair.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why gamete allele types are equally frequent
questions.stem: Brief reviewers ask why segregation guarantees equal numbers of two alleles in the gametes of a heterozygote.

options.text: Because gametes are produced in pairs, so each allele is always carried by exactly two of them.
options.misconception: invents a pairing rule for gamete production

options.text: Because the two alleles separate at meiosis, and each homologue enters half of the gametes.
Because only the dominant allele is passed on, and it fills the gametes it enters.
options.misconception: claims only the dominant allele enters gametes

options.text: Because the recessive allele is copied twice as often as the dominant one.
options.misconception: believes allele copy numbers are deliberately unequal

questions.explanation: Meiosis separates the paired homologous chromosomes, and half the gametes receive one homologue while half receive the other. Those homologues carry the two alleles, so gamete types are equal.
questions.hint: Half the gametes get each homologue.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare observed counts with an expected phenotype ratio
questions.stem: A brief records 90 plants, of which 63 show the dominant flower colour and 27 show the recessive colour.

options.text: The counts fit a 3:1 ratio, so the cross most likely involved two heterozygous parents.
The counts fit a 1:1 ratio, so the dominant parent must have been homozygous.
options.misconception: reads a near three to one split as a one to one ratio

options.text: The counts fit a 9:3:3:1 ratio, so two genes must be segregating together here.
options.misconception: claims a dihybrid ratio from one measured trait

options.text: The counts fit a 1:2:1 ratio, so the dominant class contains two genotype classes.
options.misconception: mistakes a phenotypic split for a genotypic ratio

questions.explanation: Sixty-three is about seven tenths of ninety and twenty-seven about three tenths, close to the 3:1 ratio expected from two heterozygous parents. A 1:1 or 1:2:1 pattern would need very different counts.
questions.hint: Compare the two counts with a three to one split.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Reject a claim of a guaranteed percentage
questions.stem: A brief is rejected because it says a monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes always yields exactly 75 percent dominant offspring.

options.text: The brief is right, because the dominant phenotype always covers three quarters of every brood.
options.misconception: treats an expected proportion as an exact count

options.text: The brief should say the ratio is 3:1 in the genotypic classes as well as the phenotypes.
options.misconception: confuses the genotypic ratio with the phenotypic one

options.text: The brief should say heterozygous offspring always show the recessive phenotype instead.
options.misconception: claims heterozygotes show the recessive phenotype

options.text: The brief is wrong, because 3:1 is an expected ratio and real broods vary around it.

questions.explanation: The 3:1 figure is the expectation from segregation and random gamete pairing, so a brood of any size can fall above or below it. Dominance does not change allele frequencies in the offspring, it only decides which phenotype is seen.
questions.hint: Expected proportions are not guaranteed counts.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count offspring showing one dominant and one recessive trait
questions.stem: The brief asks how many of 320 offspring of two double heterozygotes should show the first dominant trait and the second recessive trait.
questions.explanation: In a dihybrid cross the class with one dominant and one recessive trait is three sixteenths of the offspring. Three sixteenths of 320 is 60, so the brief should forecast 60 offspring in that class.
questions.hint: That class is three sixteenths of the cross.

questions.learningObjective: Count expected recessive offspring in a testcross
questions.stem: One calculation in the brief asks how many of 72 testcross offspring from a heterozygous parent would show the recessive phenotype.
questions.explanation: A testcross of a heterozygote with a homozygous recessive gives a 1:1 phenotypic ratio, so half of the 72 offspring show the recessive phenotype. Half of 72 is 36.
questions.hint: Half the offspring match the tester plant.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Derive the 3:1 ratio from a monohybrid cross
questions.stem: The team is asked to write out why a 3:1 phenotypic ratio is expected in a monohybrid cross.

answer.exemplar: Two heterozygous parents each make gametes carrying the dominant allele and the recessive allele in equal numbers. Random pairing of those gametes gives one quarter homozygous dominant, one half heterozygous and one quarter homozygous recessive. Since the heterozygotes show the dominant trait, three quarters of the offspring look dominant and one quarter looks recessive.

questions.explanation: Segregation and random gamete pairing produce one quarter, one half and one quarter of the three genotype classes, and dominance merges the first two into one visible group. That merge is what produces the three to one split.
questions.hint: Merge the two genotype classes that look alike.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State what a genotypic ratio counts
questions.stem: A requirement in the design brief asks the team to state what a genotypic ratio records in a cross of two heterozygotes.

options.text: It records the relative numbers of allele pair classes among the offspring of the cross.
It records the relative numbers of visible trait classes among the offspring of the cross.
options.misconception: defines a genotypic ratio using visible traits

options.text: It records the relative numbers of gamete types that each parent produced.
options.misconception: describes the gametes of parents rather than offspring genotypes

options.text: It records the number of chromosomes each parent contributed to the offspring.
options.misconception: confuses allele pairs with inherited chromosome numbers

questions.explanation: A genotypic ratio counts offspring by their allele pairs, so two heterozygotes produce 1:2:1. A phenotypic ratio counts by traits seen, and a gamete ratio describes what the parents produce.
questions.hint: Ask whether allele pairs or visible traits are counted.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why probabilities multiply for independent events
questions.stem: Brief reviewers ask why the product rule gives the probability of a combined outcome.

options.text: Because the outcomes are added together whenever two genes are involved in one cross.
options.misconception: claims combined probabilities are added, not multiplied

options.text: Because two independent events happening together require both, so their probabilities multiply.
Because the probability of the second outcome replaces the probability of the first.
options.misconception: believes the second probability replaces the first

options.text: Because the smaller of the two probabilities always becomes the combined answer.
options.misconception: thinks the smaller probability sets the combined value

questions.explanation: For independent events, the chance that both occur is the first probability times the second, because both must happen. Adding would wrongly count cases where only one of the events occurs.
questions.hint: Both events must happen, so multiply.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count plants carrying a given allele
questions.stem: A brief surveys 600 plants and finds 150 are AA, 300 are Aa and 150 are aa in the tracked gene.

options.text: The population carries three alleles at the locus, because three genotype classes were recorded.
options.misconception: confuses genotype classes with different alleles

options.text: All 600 plants carry allele a, because every plant was scored for it.
options.misconception: ignores that only some plants hold the allele

options.text: Only the 150 aa plants carry allele a, because heterozygotes are counted as carrying only A.
options.misconception: excludes carriers from the allele count

options.text: 450 plants carry at least one copy of allele a, made up of the 300 heterozygotes and 150 aa plants.

questions.explanation: An allele count includes every plant holding at least one copy, so the 300 heterozygotes and 150 homozygous recessive plants both carry allele a, giving 450. Three genotype classes come from two alleles, not three.
questions.hint: Count every plant with at least one copy.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim about intermediate phenotypes
questions.stem: One draft paragraph is returned because it says a pink-flowered plant must carry a pink allele in its genotype.

options.text: The brief is fine, because flower colour alleles always match the colour of the bloom.
options.misconception: assumes a phenotype must have a matching named allele

options.text: The brief should say the plant carries the dominant allele twice to produce pink blooms.
options.misconception: explains pink colour by doubling the dominant allele

options.text: The brief is wrong, because an intermediate phenotype can arise from two alleles with partial dominance.
The brief should say the plant's environment must contain the pigment needed for pink.
options.misconception: explains the phenotype by pigment supply rather than alleles

questions.explanation: An intermediate colour often comes from incomplete dominance, where a heterozygote shows a blend rather than the dominant trait. Alleles still produce the effect, and the environment can shift the shade.
questions.hint: Think about incomplete dominance between two alleles.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the allele frequency in gametes
questions.stem: A calculation asks for the fraction of gametes from a heterozygous plant that will carry the dominant allele.
questions.explanation: Segregation separates the paired alleles so that half the gametes receive one homologue and half the other. For a heterozygote, that means half the gametes carry the dominant allele and half carry the recessive one.
questions.hint: Segregation splits the two alleles evenly.

questions.learningObjective: Count dominant phenotypes in a monohybrid cross
questions.stem: Another brief asks how many of 80 offspring from a cross of two heterozygotes should show the dominant trait.
questions.explanation: Dominance makes three quarters of the offspring of two heterozygotes show the dominant trait, because the heterozygotes are grouped with the homozygous dominants. Three quarters of 80 is 60 offspring.
questions.hint: Dominant offspring are three quarters of the total.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Write out the expected results of a heterozygous cross
questions.stem: A written answer in the brief explains the expected results of crossing two heterozygous plants.

answer.exemplar: Crossing two heterozygotes, Aa with Aa, gives offspring in a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio: one quarter homozygous dominant, one half heterozygous and one quarter homozygous recessive. Because the dominant allele is expressed in the heterozygote, the phenotypic ratio is 3 dominant to 1 recessive, and the recessive class appears in every generation whenever a recessive allele is present.

questions.explanation: The gametes of each parent come in two equal types, and random pairing gives one to two to one of the genotype classes. Dominance merges the first two classes visually, so three quarters look dominant and one quarter recessive.
questions.hint: Gamete ratios lead to genotype ratios and then phenotypes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Define a dihybrid cross and its expected ratio
questions.stem: Design reviewers want the team to explain what a dihybrid cross studies and what ratio it predicts.

options.text: It studies one gene and predicts a 3:1 phenotypic ratio in the second generation of the cross.
options.misconception: describes a monohybrid cross instead of a dihybrid

options.text: It studies two genes and predicts a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio because only one gene is scored.
options.misconception: gives a single-gene ratio for a two-gene cross

options.text: It studies two genes and predicts a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio when the genes assort independently.
It studies three genes and predicts a 1:6:15:20:15:6:1 ratio in every cross.
options.misconception: claims a three-gene ratio for a two-gene cross

questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross follows two genes, and independent assortment produces the 9:3:3:1 frequencies of allele combinations. The term counts gene pairs, so one-gene and three-gene ratios do not apply.
questions.hint: The name counts the gene pairs involved.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a testcross gives more information
questions.stem: Brief reviewers ask why a testcross gives more information than a cross between two heterozygotes.

options.text: Because the testcross uses a homozygous dominant plant, so every trait looks the same in offspring.
options.misconception: claims the tester is homozygous dominant

options.text: Because the recessive tester exposes the unknown parent's alleles instead of hiding them behind dominance.
Because a testcross produces far more offspring than a monohybrid cross can produce.
options.misconception: believes testcrosses yield more offspring by nature

options.text: Because the recessive tester guarantees that only one gene is segregating in the cross.
options.misconception: restricts testcrosses to single gene inheritance

questions.explanation: In a heterozygote by heterozygote cross, dominance hides the recessive alleles behind the dominant phenotype. A recessive tester cannot mask anything, so the offspring phenotypes report the unknown parent's gametes directly.
questions.hint: Think about which parent can mask a recessive allele.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret counts that include an intermediate class
questions.stem: A brief counts 200 seedlings and finds 148 tall, 44 short and 8 with a pale intermediate colour.

options.text: The tall and short counts match a 3:1 ratio, with the pale plants suggesting incomplete dominance.
The counts match a 1:2:1 ratio, so the brief should report genotypic classes for all three colours.
options.misconception: reads a phenotypic split as a genotypic ratio

options.text: The counts match a 9:3:3:1 ratio, so two genes must be influencing the height of each plant.
options.misconception: claims a dihybrid ratio from one height trait

options.text: The counts match a 1:1 ratio, so the brief should assume the tall parent was heterozygous.
options.misconception: claims a one to one split where three to one fits better

questions.explanation: The 148 to 44 split is close to three to one, fitting a monohybrid cross, and the pale class fits heterozygotes with incomplete dominance. A 9:3:3:1 ratio would need two scored traits.
questions.hint: Check the tall to short split against three to one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a conflation of genotypic and phenotypic ratios
questions.stem: A brief wrongly states that two heterozygous parents produce offspring with a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio.

options.text: The brief is right, because the three genotype classes are visible in the offspring.
options.misconception: assumes genotype classes are directly visible

options.text: The brief should say the phenotypic ratio is 1:2:1 only when the genes are linked.
options.misconception: restricts the genotypic ratio to linked genes

options.text: The brief should say genotypic and phenotypic ratios are the same thing by definition.
options.misconception: claims both ratios are identical by definition

options.text: The brief is wrong, because 1:2:1 is the genotypic ratio while the phenotypic ratio is 3:1.

questions.explanation: The 1:2:1 ratio counts allele pairs, so the two classes sharing the dominant phenotype are counted separately. Sorting by visible trait merges them, giving 3:1.
questions.hint: Sort by what the plants look like, not by their alleles.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count the double dominant class in a dihybrid cross
questions.stem: The brief asks how many of 64 offspring from two double heterozygous parents should show both dominant traits.
questions.explanation: The product rule gives nine sixteenths for the class showing both dominant traits in a dihybrid cross of double heterozygotes. Nine sixteenths of 64 is 36 offspring.
questions.hint: Nine sixteenths of the cross shows both traits.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count possible genotypes for a gene with three alleles
questions.stem: One question in the brief asks how many distinct genotypes a diploid organism can have for a gene with three alleles.
questions.explanation: Three alleles give the homozygous pairs AA, BB and CC, plus the three heterozygous pairs AB, AC and BC. Order within a pair does not matter, so the total is six distinct genotypes.
questions.hint: Count homozygous pairs plus heterozygous pairs.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how genotype and phenotype are connected
questions.stem: A short answer in the brief explains how genotype and phenotype are connected in an organism.

answer.exemplar: Genotype is the set of alleles an organism carries at a locus, and phenotype is the characteristic that those alleles produce in a particular environment. Because environmental conditions can change how strongly a trait is expressed, two organisms with the same genotype can show different phenotypes, and one organism can show different phenotypes in different environments.

questions.explanation: Genotype fixes the alleles, phenotype records the resulting trait, and environment can modify expression. The link is predictable but not one to one, so the same genotype need not look the same everywhere.
questions.hint: Ask whether the trait could change with the conditions.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State the practical consequence of segregation
questions.stem: A requirement in the brief states the practical consequence of the law of segregation for the breeding plan.

options.text: Each gamete carries only one allele of a gene, so offspring receive a single allele from each parent.
Each gamete carries a matched pair of alleles, so offspring receive a complete set from each parent.
options.misconception: claims gametes carry matched allele pairs

options.text: Each offspring receives two alleles of the gene from a single parent only.
options.misconception: claims one parent supplies both alleles

options.text: Each gamete carries the dominant allele whenever the parent shows the dominant trait.
options.misconception: ties allele content to the parent's visible trait

questions.explanation: Segregation means the paired alleles separate when gametes form, so each gamete carries one allele and each offspring receives one from each parent. A parent's visible trait says nothing about a gamete's allele.
questions.hint: One allele per gamete, one per parent per offspring.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Separate dominance from allele frequency
questions.stem: Brief reviewers ask why dominance does not predict how common an allele will be in a population.

options.text: Because dominance is measured only in laboratory crosses and never in natural populations.
options.misconception: restricts dominance measurements to laboratory crosses

options.text: Because dominance affects how an allele is expressed while allele frequency depends on selection and drift.
Because recessive alleles are always more common than dominant ones in every population.
options.misconception: claims recessive alleles are always more common

options.text: Because a dominant allele can never spread through a population over many generations.
options.misconception: says dominant alleles can never increase in frequency

questions.explanation: Dominance describes expression in a heterozygote, so it says nothing about how common an allele becomes. Frequencies respond to selection, migration, drift and mutation, all independent of dominance.
questions.hint: Expression and population frequency are separate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare two crosses that used different parents
questions.stem: A brief compares two crosses of the same plant, one giving 24 tall and 26 short and the other 49 tall and 11 short.

options.text: The first cross shows a 1:2:1 ratio, so the tall parent must have been homozygous.
options.misconception: reads a one to one split as a genotypic ratio

options.text: The second cross shows a 9:3:3:1 ratio, so two genes must segregate in that cross.
options.misconception: claims a dihybrid ratio from a single trait

options.text: The first cross shows a 3:1 ratio, so the second cross must have had two heterozygous parents.
options.misconception: assigns the three to one ratio to the wrong cross

options.text: The first cross fits a 1:1 ratio and the second a 3:1 ratio, matching two different parental genotypes.

questions.explanation: Twenty-four to twenty-six is close to 1:1, which fits a heterozygote crossed with a homozygous recessive. Forty-nine to eleven is close to 3:1, which fits two heterozygous parents, so the two crosses used different parents.
questions.hint: Compare each split with a one to one or three to one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim of equal phenotype classes
questions.stem: A brief claims that a dihybrid cross between double heterozygotes always produces equal numbers of each phenotype.

options.text: The claim holds, because independent assortment spreads the offspring evenly across phenotypes.
options.misconception: confuses independent assortment with equal proportions

options.text: The claim should say the ratio is 1:1:1:1 whenever the two genes are unlinked.
options.misconception: claims unlinked genes give equal phenotype classes

options.text: The claim is wrong, because independent assortment predicts 9:3:3:1 rather than equal classes.
The claim should say equal numbers appear only in the third generation of the cross.
options.misconception: places equal classes in the third generation

questions.explanation: Independent assortment makes all gene combinations possible, but not equally likely: the double dominant combination covers nine of sixteen gamete pairings. The prediction is 9:3:3:1, not four equal classes.
questions.hint: More combinations give the double dominant class.

questions.learningObjective: Count expected recessive offspring in a testcross
questions.stem: A calculation in the brief asks for the expected number of recessive offspring in a testcross with 90 offspring.
questions.explanation: A testcross of a heterozygote with a homozygous recessive gives a 1:1 phenotypic ratio, so half of the offspring show the recessive trait. Half of 90 is 45.
questions.hint: Half the offspring match the recessive tester.

questions.learningObjective: Count recessive offspring from a 3:1 ratio
questions.stem: A count in the brief asks how many of 400 seedlings from two heterozygous parents should show the recessive trait.
questions.explanation: A 3:1 phenotypic ratio puts one quarter of the offspring in the recessive class. One quarter of 400 is 100 seedlings.
questions.hint: One quarter of the offspring show the recessive trait.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Derive the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio
questions.stem: One model answer in the brief states how the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio is derived from a cross.

answer.exemplar: Each heterozygous parent makes two kinds of gamete in equal numbers, one carrying the dominant allele and one carrying the recessive allele. Any gamete from one parent can pair with any gamete from the other, so the homozygous dominant combination takes one quarter of the offspring, the heterozygous combination takes one half and the homozygous recessive combination takes one quarter.

questions.explanation: Equal gamete types from both parents, paired at random, produce four equally likely combinations. Those group into one homozygous dominant class, two equal heterozygous classes and one homozygous recessive class.
questions.hint: Count the four possible gamete pairings first.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State the condition for multiplying probabilities
questions.stem: Design reviewers want a statement about when two probabilities may be multiplied together.

options.text: Probabilities multiply whenever two traits are observed on the same organism in one visit.
options.misconception: treats shared measurement as evidence of independence

options.text: Probabilities multiply only when the two outcomes belong to different organisms.
options.misconception: requires different organisms for events to be independent

options.text: Probabilities multiply for independent events, where one does not affect the other.
Probabilities multiply for mutually exclusive events, where only one can occur.
options.misconception: confuses mutually exclusive events with independent ones

questions.explanation: The product rule applies to independent events, whose outcomes do not influence one another, so allele combinations come from multiplying single-gene probabilities. Mutually exclusive events are added instead.
questions.hint: Check that one event does not change the other.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe where alleles sit on homologous chromosomes
questions.stem: Brief reviewers ask how alleles relate to a gene's position on a chromosome.

options.text: Each allele occupies a different position, so a chromosome can hold several copies of one gene.
options.misconception: believes alleles sit at separate positions on one chromosome

options.text: Each allele occupies the same locus on a different homologue of the same chromosome type.
Alleles are carried inside the nucleus only, and never appear in the cytoplasm.
options.misconception: claims alleles never appear in the cytoplasm

options.text: Alleles are produced only during cell division, and disappear between divisions.
options.misconception: claims alleles are created and destroyed each division

questions.explanation: Alleles are versions of one gene sitting at the same locus on the two homologous chromosomes. They are inherited rather than remade each division, and transcripts of them can appear in the cytoplasm.
questions.hint: Picture one locus on two matching chromosomes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Match genotype classes to observed phenotypes
questions.stem: A brief lists plants with genotypes AA, Aa, Aa and aa and records their heights as tall, tall, tall and short.

options.text: The heights show a 3:1 phenotypic ratio, and the two genotypes that look alike are AA and Aa.
The heights show a 3:1 phenotypic ratio, so the brief should count only the short plant in later summaries.
options.misconception: suggests dropping a class from the summary

options.text: The heights show a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio, so the brief should report three phenotype classes.
options.misconception: calls a phenotype split a genotypic ratio

options.text: The heights show a 9:3:3:1 ratio, so the brief should add a second scored trait.
options.misconception: claims a dihybrid ratio from four plants

questions.explanation: Three tall and one short gives the 3:1 phenotypic ratio, while the allele pairs give 1:2:1. The tall class holds both homozygous dominant and heterozygous plants, because dominance masks the recessive allele.
questions.hint: Group the plants by how they look, not by their alleles.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim about gamete allele content
questions.stem: A brief states that a plant heterozygous for a gene passes both of its alleles to a quarter of its gametes.

options.text: The brief is right, because the two alleles are copied before they are separated.
options.misconception: blames allele copying for the gamete contents

options.text: The brief should say the plant passes both alleles to every one of its gametes.
options.misconception: claims every gamete carries both alleles

options.text: The brief should say the plant passes only the dominant allele to three quarters of its gametes.
options.misconception: invents a gamete ratio tied to dominance

options.text: The brief is wrong, because each gamete receives one allele, with a half chance for each kind.

questions.explanation: Segregation sends one allele into each gamete, so a heterozygous plant produces equal numbers of the two gamete types rather than passing both at once. Dominance affects which phenotype appears, not which allele a gamete carries.
questions.hint: One allele per gamete, in equal numbers.

questions.learningObjective: Count dominant offspring from a homozygous cross
questions.stem: One estimate in the brief asks how many of 50 offspring from a homozygous dominant crossed with a heterozygous plant show the dominant trait.
questions.explanation: Every gamete from the homozygous dominant parent carries the dominant allele, so every offspring shows the dominant trait whatever the heterozygote contributes. All 50 look dominant.
questions.hint: One parent always supplies the dominant allele.

questions.explanation: A heterozygote crossed with a homozygous recessive gives a 1:1 phenotypic ratio, so half of the 240 offspring show the dominant trait. Half of 240 is 120.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: List the assumptions behind a 9:3:3:1 prediction
questions.stem: A short written answer explains why the assumptions behind a predicted 9:3:3:1 ratio matter.

answer.exemplar: The prediction assumes the two genes assort independently, that each parent is heterozygous for both genes, that the alleles show complete dominance and that gamete pairing is random. If any of these fails, the observed ratio will differ, for example a 1:2:1 ratio when the genes are linked, or a modified ratio for incomplete dominance.

questions.explanation: The 9:3:3:1 ratio needs independent assortment, two heterozygous parents, complete dominance and random pairing. Linkage, incomplete dominance or a different parental genotype each shift the expected proportions.
questions.hint: List the conditions before trusting the ratio.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Read a testcross ratio as evidence of genotype
questions.stem: The design reviewer wants a correct statement about the offspring ratio of a testcross.

options.text: A 1:1 split of dominant and recessive offspring means the unknown parent was heterozygous.
A 1:1 split of offspring means the unknown parent was homozygous dominant.
options.misconception: reads a testcross split as complete dominance

options.text: An all dominant brood means the unknown parent was heterozygous for the trait.
options.misconception: assigns heterozygosity to an all dominant brood

options.text: An all recessive brood means the tester plant was homozygous dominant.
options.misconception: misassigns the tester genotype in a recessive brood

questions.explanation: The recessive tester contributes only recessive alleles, so dominant offspring reveal a dominant allele from the unknown parent. Half and half means the unknown made both gamete types, which only a heterozygote does.
questions.hint: Use the tester phenotype to read the offspring.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Relate phenotypic and genotypic ratios in a dihybrid cross
questions.stem: Brief reviewers ask how the phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross relates to the genotypic ratio.

options.text: They are always identical, because each genotype produces a separate visible trait.
options.misconception: believes every genotype shows a distinct visible trait

options.text: The phenotypic ratio merges genotype classes that look alike, reporting 9:3:3:1 rather than sixteen genotypes.
The phenotypic ratio is always 1:1, because the two genes assort independently.
options.misconception: claims independent assortment forces equal phenotype classes

options.text: Neither ratio can be predicted before the offspring are scored in the field.
options.misconception: says neither ratio can be predicted beforehand

questions.explanation: Sixteen allele pairings arise in a dihybrid cross, but they collapse into four visible classes because dominance groups genotypes that look alike. The genotypic ratio lists sixteen classes, the phenotypic four.
questions.hint: Count the visible classes rather than the pairings.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Test a genotypic count against the 1:2:1 ratio
questions.stem: A brief scores genotypes for 200 seedlings and finds 100 heterozygous and 100 homozygous offspring in total.

options.text: The counts fit the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio, since the heterozygous half should be twice either homozygous class.
The counts fit the 3:1 phenotypic ratio, since one quarter of the seedlings should look recessive.
options.misconception: reads a genotypic count as a phenotypic split

options.text: The counts fit the 9:3:3:1 ratio, since sixteen allele pairings are possible in a dihybrid cross.
options.misconception: claims a dihybrid ratio from one gene's genotypes

options.text: The counts fit the 1:1 ratio expected from a cross of a heterozygote with a recessive plant.
options.misconception: applies a testcross ratio to a two-heterozygote cross

questions.explanation: In a 1:2:1 ratio the homozygous classes are one part each and the heterozygous class two parts, so with 200 seedlings the heterozygous group should be about 100, as recorded. A 1:1 split would fit a testcross.
questions.hint: Split the total into one, two and one parts.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Reject a fixed-count claim about a ratio term
questions.stem: One claim in the brief asserts that a dihybrid cross of double heterozygotes must give exactly 9 double dominant offspring.

options.text: The claim holds, because the double dominant class always takes nine parts of sixteen.
options.misconception: treats a ratio part as a literal offspring count

options.text: The claim should say eight double dominant offspring, because eight allele combinations exist.
options.misconception: confuses the number of allele combinations with offspring

options.text: The claim holds, because independent assortment fixes the size of each phenotype class.
options.misconception: believes independent assortment fixes class sizes exactly

options.text: The claim is wrong, because 9:3:3:1 gives an expected proportion, not a fixed number of offspring.

questions.explanation: The nine in 9:3:3:1 is a share of the whole, so the double dominant class holds about nine sixteenths of the offspring but never a fixed number. Only large broods make the count look exact.
questions.hint: Ratios give shares, not literal counts.
